summary: Deep technical session focused on GPU runtime kernel selection and profiling. Discussed kernel-level differences between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, CUDA graph utilization, KV cache behavior, batching strategies and implications for latency/throughput. Agreed next steps to share CUDA graphs, run a short vLLM baseline on customer infra, and review Dedicated vs Hosted economics and VPC requirements.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're going to dive into kernel selection and profiler outputs across TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, and show some CUDA graphs. Priya will take the runbook on the profiler bits.
[00:12] Tom Reyes: Yep, thanks, Alex. Quick context: we're evaluating options for low-latency chat inference, target p95 < 120ms for 1k tokens workloads, we have 4xA100 on prem behind a VPC.
[00:25] Priya Patel: Great. We'll start with a high-level: kernel selection in our runtime picks different GEMM / attention kernels depending on model size, head dims, and sequence length distribution. Some of that is automatic in TensorRT-LLM, vLLM picks kernels differently and sometimes falls back to generic cuBLAS for certain shapes.
[00:42] Lisa Nguyen: when you say "picks" — is that dynamic at runtime or compile time? We saw something earlier where the kernel changed mid-stream.
[00:49] Priya Patel: Good question. For TensorRT-LLM it's mostly graph compile time + heuristics, so it can be more static; for vLLM with our runtime wrappers it can be dynamic per-request if you enable kernel auto-selection. That dynamic switch can introduce jitter if your sequence lengths vary a lot.
[01:05] Marco Silva: we observed higher tail latencies when batches had mixed lengths, is that the same issue?
[01:08] Priya Patel: Exactly, mixed-length batching + dynamic kernel selection = non-deterministic kernels chosen which impacts p95/p99. Also KV cache management matters: if you don't pin cache to GPU memory or you have host spill, you pay context-switch costs.
[01:22] Alex Chen: we'll show a CUDA graph from a TensorRT-LLM run followed by a vLLM trace to highlight where the stalls are. Priya, can you share screen?
[01:30] Priya Patel: sharing. Ok first slide is a TensorRT-LLM CUDA Graph: you can see the load is very compact, kernels are fused, attention + ffn ops collapsed into fewer launches — fewer kernel launches means lower kernel launch overhead but longer per-kernel runtime.
[01:46] Priya Patel: Note the big purple blocks here, those are attention fused kernels; they amortize launch overhead but if you hit a path that isn't fused we jump to many small kernels.
[01:54] Anya Petrov: I'm seeing some misses annotated as "kv chache spill" in the profiler — is that from evictions or something else?
[01:59] Priya Patel: Likely cache eviction due to small per-GPU memory windows. In some of your configs we saw KV cache stored in pageable memory accidentally. That causes PCIe roundtrips.
[02:10] Tom Reyes: We do have some swaps when we run concurrent encoders + decoder workloads. How aggressive is Redwood's KV pinning option?
[02:16] Alex Chen: We have a config for pinning KV cache to GPU and reserving a little headroom so it doesn't get swapped out during bursts. In Dedicated we can lock that down. On Hosted we recommend similar flags but you need to ensure your model shard sizes fit.
[02:28] Priya Patel: Back to kernel selection — vLLM tends to use more small kernels but benefits from better pipelining in some cases. TensorRT-LLM's fused kernels show better throughput for long sequences but can cost higher single-token latency for some shapes.
[02:41] Lisa Nguyen: can you quantify? like throughput tokens/sec or p95 numbers?
[02:45] Priya Patel: From our lab runs on A100 80GB: TensorRT-LLM fused runs got about 1.6x tokens/sec for 2k sequence workloads compared to the vLLM baseline, but p95 for single-turn 256-token chat often favored vLLM by ~10-20ms because of lighter-weight kernels. Those numbers vary with batch size and prompt prefix lengths.
[03:04] Marco Silva: those are lab numbers. On-prem we have variability due to noisy neighbor workloads; any tips to stabilize?
[03:10] Priya Patel: Use CUDA graphs to capture steady-state sequences — record a CUDA graph for the typical request pattern and replay it. It eliminates kernel launch overhead and dynamic kernel selection. But graphs are brittle if you change sequence length or model shape frequently.
[03:23] Alex Chen: Also our runtime supports fallback graphs and multi-graph strategies — we record a few common lengths and route requests to the closest graph. That reduces the graph brittleness.
[03:33] Tom Reyes: Ok, show us the actual graph timings.
[03:36] Priya Patel: (sharing profiler) here's TensorRT-LLM CUDA Graph timeline: you see two dominant kernels accounting for ~65% of runtime — the fused attention and fused FFN. Kernel launch counts are low. There's almost no memcpy except initial inputs.
[03:50] Priya Patel: here's vLLM trace: many more kernels, higher launch count, but each kernel is shorter. You can see small gaps where the runtime decides kernel selection — those gaps align with slight p95 spikes.
[04:05] Lisa Nguyen: in the vLLM trace there are some kernel stalls labeled "context sync" — what's that?
[04:09] Priya Patel: That's the CPU-GPU synchronization where we do KV cache updates on host threads. If your KV cache is on host or synchronized more often, you pay these syncs. We recommend keeping KV cache resident on GPU and using async copies only when necessary.
[04:22] Anya Petrov: what about quantization — do kernels change when running int8 or 4-bit quantized weights?
[04:27] Priya Patel: Yes. Quantized kernels often use specialized int8/4-bit GEMM kernels which are different code paths — TensorRT has excellent fused int8 kernels, vLLM relies on custom quant kernels which may not be fused as aggressively. That can change both throughput and latency characteristics. The tradeoff is lower memory and higher throughput but you must validate for quality.
[04:45] Marco Silva: we care about worst-case tail for SLAs. If we move to 4-bit quant, will tail get worse?
[04:49] Priya Patel: Not necessarily — it can improve tail because compute is faster, but if quantized kernels are less fused and create more kernel launches, you could see more launch overhead. Using CUDA graphs with quantized kernels often gives the best of both worlds.
[05:02] Tom Reyes: any gotchas for CUDA graphs on multi-GPU?
[05:06] Priya Patel: With multi-GPU you need to record graphs per device and ensure your NVLink peer-access patterns are stable. Also watch out for NCCL collectives — graphs don't capture dynamic NCCL topology changes. For distributed sharding we recommend recording a graph per shard configuration.
[05:21] Alex Chen: let's pivot to an example we ran last week — we tested 13B model with both runtimes. Priya, quick numbers?
[05:26] Priya Patel: Sure: 13B on 4xA100, sequence 2k, batch size 4: TensorRT-LLM w/ fused kernels + CUDA graphs = ~1.6x tokens/sec vs vLLM baseline. Tail p95 improved ~12% after graphing. Without graphs, TensorRT had slightly higher single-token latency at small batch sizes.
[05:43] Lisa Nguyen: You mentioned earlier that vLLM has dynamic kernel selection. Could we force static picks to reduce jitter?
[05:49] Priya Patel: You can pin kernels in vLLM by building with targeted kernel flags or by pre-warming specific paths. Another approach: use workload-aware batching with homogeneous lengths. That is, avoid length-mixed batches for low-latency requests.
[06:01] Marco Silva: what about memory consumption with fused kernels? Is it higher?
[06:04] Priya Patel: Fused kernels sometimes require additional scratch buffers, but TensorRT is good about reusing workspace. It can be slightly higher but often worth the throughput gains. Monitor peak memory in the profiler.
[06:16] Tom Reyes: can Redwood's Dedicated offering help here? e.g., reserve memory and pin KV?
[06:20] Alex Chen: yes. Dedicated lets you configure node-level reservations, KG cache pinning, and we can coordinate cross-tenant scheduling to avoid noisy neighbors. For on-prem we ship an agent that exposes similar flags if you want Redwood-managed runtime.
[06:32] Anya Petrov: Regarding PCIe vs NVLink — our cluster uses NVLink, will that change recommendations?
[06:37] Priya Patel: NVLink reduces inter-GPU transfer costs and makes KV cross-device access much faster. With NVLink you can be more aggressive with model parallelism and shard KV across GPUs. If you have only PCIe, avoid frequent cross-device KV accesses.
[06:48] Lisa Nguyen: About profiler outputs — what should we upload to you so you can help analyze?
[06:52] Priya Patel: Please send: CUDA graph captures (.cudagraph), nvprof / Nsight timings, the GPU kernel timeline screenshot, the allocator logs showing memory peaks, and the vLLM/TensorRT-LLM config files. We'll also ask for representative request traces (anonymized).
[07:06] Tom Reyes: We'll need a checklist to gather these.
[07:09] Alex Chen: we'll assemble a checklist and share a shared sheet (we have a benchmark sheet link). I'll drop the sheet after this call.
[07:17] Priya Patel: One more thing: batching policies — if you want lower p95, prefer smaller batches but with KV caching to keep throughput. For throughput cost optimization, larger batches + fused kernels + graphs is best. It's always a tradeoff.
[07:31] Marco Silva: Are there any quick config flags we can toggle to see immediate improvements?
[07:35] Priya Patel: Yep: 1) enable KV pinning (gpu_kv_pin=true), 2) set batcher max wait to 10ms for low-latency, 3) enable CUDA graph recording for stable request shapes, 4) enable mixed precision kernels if not already. We'll share recommended defaults.
[07:51] Lisa Nguyen: How brittle is graph recording if we update model weights or quantize?
[07:55] Priya Patel: If you change the model's operator shapes (for instance with new head dims) you'll need to re-record. Quantization often changes kernel code paths, so re-record after quantization. Small scaler changes usually ok.
[08:07] Tom Reyes: security question — on our VPC, are there extra steps for collecting profiler artifacts? We can't upload raw traces externally.
[08:13] Alex Chen: Understood. We can provide an on-prem collection script and you can sanitize logs before uploading. For sensitive runs we can run joint sessions where you screen-share profiler output. We'll also send our security doc for artifact handling.
[08:28] Lisa Nguyen: any recommendations for long-term monitoring to catch regressions?
[08:33] Priya Patel: Instrument kernel launch counts, average kernel durations, KV cache miss rate, and p95/p99 latencies. Redwood's Console can surface these with alerts if you instrument traces. But you can start with Prometheus metrics and Nsight periodic captures.
[08:48] Alex Chen: Ok let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[08:51] Priya Patel: Recap: 1) shared differences between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM kernel strategies; 2) CUDA graphs can remove launch overhead and stabilize tail but are brittle; 3) KV cache pinning and correct memory placement is critical; 4) quantization changes kernel code paths and should be validated for quality and perf.
[09:08] Alex Chen: Next steps: Priya will upload example CUDA graphs and notes; Tom & team will run the vLLM baseline and upload logs; Alex will send Dedicated vs Hosted cost/throughput scenarios and the security checklist. We'll reconvene after baseline results.
[09:25] Tom Reyes: Thanks all, that was helpful. We'll try to get the baseline running this week.
[09:29] Lisa Nguyen: thanks, bye.
[09:31] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, bye.
